analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits for retirees, widows, and widowers, paid for by taxing high earners' income above the payroll tax cap.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2019, despite 33 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would expand Social Security in three main ways: it would replace the current cost-of-living formula with one based on the prices seniors actually pay, which rise faster; it would increase the benefit formula so monthly checks grow faster; and it would raise benefits for widows and widowers in two-income households. To pay for it, it would apply the Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment income above the annual cap (about $128,400 in 2018), phasing that in fully by 2023. It was introduced in late September 2018, sent to two committees, and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees and disabled workers would see benefits rise through a richer benefit formula and cost-of-living adjustments tied to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which typically grows faster than the index used today. Widows and widowers in two-income households would get higher survivor benefits. Low-income SSI recipients would be protected from losing supplemental benefits when their Social Security checks rise.

how_it_helps.text: Changes the cost-of-living adjustment to use a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, reflecting the spending patterns of retirees, whose costs (especially health care) tend to rise faster than the general index
Raises the top factor in the benefit formula from 90 percent to 95 percent, phased in from 2023 to 2027, and adds a 5 percent credit on earnings above the old cap, increasing monthly benefits
Replaces the widow's or widower's benefit with the greater of the deceased spouse's benefit or 75 percent of the combined couple's benefits, improving survivor income in two-income households
Holds SSI beneficiaries harmless so the higher Social Security payments do not reduce their supplemental income

analysis.who_pays: High-income workers and the self-employed. Under current law, wages above the annual cap (about $128,400 in 2018) are exempt from the Social Security payroll tax; this bill would tax 80 percent of income above the cap starting in 2019, with the share rising until all above-cap income is taxable in 2023.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning over the payroll cap

drawbacks.text: It raises payroll taxes on high earners and self-employed professionals, phasing in from 80 percent of above-cap income taxed in 2019 to all of it by 2023
The new 5 percent credit on surplus earnings gives high earners back a small share of benefits on income above the cap, modestly offsetting the new revenue

Richer benefit formulas and faster-growing cost-of-living adjustments increase what the program pays out every year, so the bill trades a permanent tax increase for permanently higher outlays, and critics of lifting the cap argue it weakens the link between what workers contribute and what they receive

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit increases are broad and lasting, aimed at retirees, disabled workers, and particularly widows and widowers, and they are paid for by a tax confined to income above the cap that only high earners pay. The main honest objection is the tax itself: the wealthiest payroll earners and self-employed households would face a new tax on every dollar above roughly $128,400, and the program's costs would rise permanently. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much weight one gives to faster-growing senior benefits versus the tax burden on upper-income earners.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means and Education and Workforce committees the day it was introduced, neither committee acted, and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Linda Sánchez introduced the bill on September 27, 2018, with 30 original cosponsors, all Democrats
The Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, for relevant provisions, the Education and Workforce Committee
The bill accumulated 33 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action was ever taken on it
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households kept paying Social Security payroll tax only on income up to the annual cap, and no one had to weigh the bill's trade-offs. Retirees and widows forgo the benefit increases the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the payroll tax cap

for.name: Rep. Linda Sánchez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with 30 original Democratic cosponsors

for.name: 33 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Kevin Brady (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup

against.name: Speaker Paul Ryan
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; a bill with no committee action cannot reach the floor without the leadership scheduling it

sides.party_line_note: All 33 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committees and House leadership never acted on it.

industries.industry: High-income households (earners above the payroll tax cap)
industries.note: They would pay the Social Security payroll tax on income above roughly $128,400, phased in to full taxation by 2023; the bill's benefit increases are funded by this tax, so their cost is the public's gain. A 5 percent benefit credit on surplus earnings returns a small share to them.
The bill applies the same above-cap taxation to self-employment income, which for the self-employed means both the employee and employer share of the tax on income above the cap.
